title: How Tennis Evolved Over the Centuries
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Tennis is a very old racket sport. Most historians think the game started in northern France in the 12th century. At first, people hit the ball with their hand. This early game was called jeu de paume, which means game of the palm.
pages.caption: Players on Wimbledon's Centre Court in 2008, a year before the installation of a retractable roof

imageProvenance.credit: The original uploader was Razzle-dazzle at English Wikipedia.

evidence.articleCaption: Players on Wimbledon's Centre Court in 2008, a year before the installation of a retractable roof

pages.text: Later, players started to use a glove instead of a bare hand. By the 16th century, rackets came into use. The game then moved to enclosed areas and began to be called tennis. This older version of the sport is known today as real tennis.
pages.caption: Drawing of a lawn tennis court as originally designed by Major Walter Clopton Wingfield in 1874

evidence.articleCaption: Drawing of a lawn tennis court as originally designed by Major Walter Clopton Wingfield in 1874

pages.text: The word tennis came into English in the mid-14th century from French. It comes from the term Tenez, which can be translated as hold, receive, or take. A server would call this to his opponent to show he was about to serve.
pages.caption: Tennis racquets made of wood and CFRP (carbon fibre reinforced plastics) side by side

evidence.fileTitle: File:Tennis rackets made of wood and CFRP (carbon fibre reinforced plastics) side by side.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Tennis racquets made of wood and CFRP (carbon fibre reinforced plastics) side by side

pages.text: In the late nineteenth century, a new version called lawn tennis spread quickly. Different groups had different rules, which caused confusion. An open meeting helped create standard rules in March 1875. These rules laid the foundation for the first Wimbledon tournament in 1877.
pages.caption: Cover of the first edition of a book about lawn tennis by Walter Clopton Wingfield, published in February 1874

evidence.articleCaption: Cover of the first edition of a book about lawn tennis by Walter Clopton Wingfield, published in February 1874

pages.text: Over time, major international competitions began. The Davis Cup for men started. Later, the Federation Cup for women began. In 1968, the Open Era started, allowing professional players and amateurs to compete together in the major tournaments.

pages.text: International team competitions soon followed. Dwight F. Davis created a men's tournament in 1900 that became the Davis Cup, while a women's team competition started in 1963. For decades, professionals and amateurs remained strictly separated until the Open Era began in 1968, allowing all players to compete together in major tournaments.

C1-C2.headline: The Origins and Evolution of Tennis

pages.text: Traditionally named lawn tennis and invented in Edgbaston, Birmingham, the sport known simply as tennis is the direct descendant of real or royal tennis. Most historians suggest the precursor originated in northern France during the 12th century, initially played by striking the ball with the palm of the hand under the designation jeu de paume.
pages.caption: Players on Wimbledon's Centre Court in 2008, a year before the installation of a retractable roof

imageProvenance.credit: The original uploader was Razzle-dazzle at English Wikipedia.

evidence.articleCaption: Players on Wimbledon's Centre Court in 2008, a year before the installation of a retractable roof

pages.text: The game transitioned through the use of bare hands and gloves before racquets were introduced in the 16th century. Enclosed playing areas and stabilized rules characterized this era, which is now distinguished as real tennis. Historical accounts note that monarchs like Henry VIII were notable enthusiasts of this royal variant.
pages.caption: Drawing of a lawn tennis court as originally designed by Major Walter Clopton Wingfield in 1874

evidence.articleCaption: Drawing of a lawn tennis court as originally designed by Major Walter Clopton Wingfield in 1874

pages.text: Etymologically, the term tennis entered the English lexicon in the mid-14th century from the Anglo-Norman Tenez, signifying a server's call to receive or hold. The earliest known literary appearance in English occurs in John Gower's 1400 poem dedicated to King Henry IV, illustrating the early currency of the terminology.

pages.text: By the late 19th century, real tennis possessed a codified history, whereas lawn tennis suffered from a proliferation of competing rulebooks that generated considerable confusion. An open meeting held at Lord's in March 1875 successfully promulgated a unifying code of laws that directly enabled the inaugural Wimbledon Championships in 1877.

pages.text: Institutional structures expanded internationally with the establishment of the Davis Cup and the precursor to the Fed Cup. Promoter C.C. Pyle initiated the first professional tour in 1926, establishing a rigid divide between professionals and amateurs. This division persisted until April 1968, when the advent of the Open Era permitted professionals to contest major tournaments alongside amateurs.

title: The History and Uses of Commemorative Plaques
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: A commemorative plaque is a flat piece of metal, stone, or wood. It has words or pictures on it. It helps people remember a person, an event, or an old use of a place. Most plaques go on a wall or another tall surface.
pages.caption: Plaque in tribute to Claude Bernard at Collège de France in Paris

evidence.articleCaption: Plaque in tribute to Claude Bernard at Collège de France in Paris

pages.text: Many modern plaques show that a place is important. People can visit these spots to learn about history. Some new memorials even use QR codes. Visitors can scan the code with a smartphone to see photos, videos, and stories.
pages.caption: A Benin Bronze plaque

evidence.fileTitle: File:Benin Bronzes at the British Museum 2.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A Benin Bronze plaque

pages.text: Long ago, the Benin Empire made brass and bronze plaques. These metal plates showed important people and battles. In medieval Europe, people also made brass memorial plaques. Workers put them inside churches and on tombs.
pages.caption: An example of a lightbox used as a commemorative plaque

evidence.fileTitle: File:Louisa lawson suffragette light box memorial greenway.JPG
evidence.articleCaption: An example of a lightbox used as a commemorative plaque

pages.text: Today, many countries have special historical marker programs. In the Philippines, cast-iron markers share history all over the country. In England, famous blue plaques show where important people lived and worked.
pages.caption: A plaque commemorating the victims of a mass execution during the Axis occupation of Greece in Fregkaina, Greece

evidence.fileTitle: File:Monument to people executed in Fregkaina during German occupation.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A plaque commemorating the victims of a mass execution during the Axis occupation of Greece in Fregkaina, Greece

pages.text: Local groups and governments also put up markers to share local stories. Sometimes, people give small plaques as awards instead of trophies. These special signs help communities remember history everywhere.

B1-B2.headline: The History and Uses of Commemorative Plaques

pages.text: A commemorative plaque, also known as a historical marker, is a plate made of metal, ceramic, stone, or wood. Displaying text or relief images, these markers are typically attached to vertical surfaces to honor specific people, past events, or former uses of a location.
pages.caption: Plaque in tribute to Claude Bernard at Collège de France in Paris

evidence.articleCaption: Plaque in tribute to Claude Bernard at Collège de France in Paris

pages.text: While traditional markers simply highlight places worth visiting, twenty-first-century memorials often incorporate modern technology. Some use QR codes that visitors can scan with smartphones to access digital memorial pages featuring photographs, videos, and stories.
pages.caption: A Benin Bronze plaque

evidence.fileTitle: File:Benin Bronzes at the British Museum 2.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A Benin Bronze plaque

pages.text: The tradition of creating metal plaques dates back centuries. The Benin Empire produced brass and bronze plaques from the thirteenth through sixteenth centuries to commemorate significant historical events and figures associated with the royal court.
pages.caption: An example of a lightbox used as a commemorative plaque

evidence.fileTitle: File:Louisa lawson suffragette light box memorial greenway.JPG
evidence.articleCaption: An example of a lightbox used as a commemorative plaque

pages.text: Similarly, medieval European craftspeople manufactured brass memorial plaques to place inside churches and on tombs. Today, formal historical marker systems operate globally, managed by national preservation agencies, local governments, and independent organizations.
pages.caption: A plaque commemorating the victims of a mass execution during the Axis occupation of Greece in Fregkaina, Greece

evidence.fileTitle: File:Monument to people executed in Fregkaina during German occupation.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A plaque commemorating the victims of a mass execution during the Axis occupation of Greece in Fregkaina, Greece

pages.text: In the United Kingdom, London features a notable historical plaque scheme that is thought to be the oldest system of its kind. Meanwhile, the Philippines utilizes cast-iron markers installed by the National Historical Commission to commemorate people, places, and events across the country.

Beyond historical sites, plaques frequently serve as awards in place of traditional trophies. Whether honoring ancient rulers, celebrating modern community heritage, or recognizing individual achievements, these markers preserve important stories across generations.

C1-C2.headline: The Evolution and Global Traditions of Plaques

pages.text: Commemorative plaques, alternatively designated as historical markers, comprise plates of diverse materials such as metal, ceramic, stone, or wood. Adorned with relief imagery or text, they are affixed to vertical surfaces primarily to commemorate specific individuals, historical events, or structural antecedents.
pages.caption: Plaque in tribute to Claude Bernard at Collège de France in Paris

evidence.articleCaption: Plaque in tribute to Claude Bernard at Collège de France in Paris

pages.text: Contemporary applications extend beyond mere designation of culturally significant locations. Recent technological integration involves QR codes that facilitate interactive digital engagement, linking users to multimedia archives containing photographs, videos, and biographical narratives.
pages.caption: A Benin Bronze plaque

evidence.fileTitle: File:Benin Bronzes at the British Museum 2.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A Benin Bronze plaque

pages.text: Historically, sophisticated sculptural traditions utilized metal casting for commemoration. The Benin Empire produced intricate brass and bronze plaques between the thirteenth and sixteenth centuries, documenting court personnel and military expansion, while medieval European artisans created sepulchral brasses for ecclesiastical interiors.
pages.caption: An example of a lightbox used as a commemorative plaque

evidence.fileTitle: File:Louisa lawson suffragette light box memorial greenway.JPG
evidence.articleCaption: An example of a lightbox used as a commemorative plaque

pages.text: Institutional preservation frameworks now govern marker installation internationally. Prominent initiatives include the United Kingdom's venerable blue plaque network, established in the nineteenth century, and the extensive cast-iron marker system administered by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines.
pages.caption: A plaque commemorating the victims of a mass execution during the Axis occupation of Greece in Fregkaina, Greece

evidence.fileTitle: File:Monument to people executed in Fregkaina during German occupation.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A plaque commemorating the victims of a mass execution during the Axis occupation of Greece in Fregkaina, Greece

pages.text: Scheme administration frequently involves diverse local authorities and specialized civic societies employing distinct criteria. Consequently, regional variations emerge, ranging from color-coded urban systems to specialized commemorative rounds nominated by community stakeholders.

In addition to their socio-historical function in public spaces, plaques serve as formal tokens of achievement, frequently replacing traditional ribbons or trophies. Through these multifaceted implementations, markers continually mediate collective memory and institutional recognition.

title: History and Ruins of Taxila
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Taxila is a historic city and World Heritage Site in the Punjab province of Pakistan. Founded around 1000 BC, it is one of the oldest cities in South Asia. Today, it is a popular tourist spot that attracts up to one million visitors every year.
pages.caption: Eastern border of the Achaemenid Empire

evidence.fileTitle: File:Eastern border of the Achaemenid Empire.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Eastern border of the Achaemenid Empire

pages.text: The city was historically known as Takṣaśilā in Sanskrit. The region around Taxila was settled by the Neolithic era, with ruins dating to 1000 BCE. Early Harappan period ruins from around 1300 BCE have also been discovered in the area.
pages.caption: A map of Alexander's campaign in ancient India.

imageProvenance.credit: No machine-readable author provided. World Imaging assumed (based on copyright claims).

evidence.articleCaption: A map of Alexander's campaign in ancient India.

pages.text: During his invasion of the Indus Valley, Alexander the Great gained control of Taxila in 326 BCE after its ruler surrendered without a battle. In the following centuries, the Indo-Greeks, Indo-Scythians, Indo-Parthians, and Kushans successively made Taxila their capital city.
pages.caption: A view over the ruins of Sirkap.

evidence.articleCaption: A view over the ruins of Sirkap.

pages.text: Some scholars consider ancient Taxila to be one of the earliest education centres in South Asia. It had great influence on Hindu culture and the Sanskrit language. The strategist Chanakya and the grammarian Pāṇini were both part of the community at Taxila.
pages.caption: The Dharmarajika Stupa

evidence.articleCaption: The Dharmarajika Stupa

pages.text: In the fifth century, the invading Hunas devastated the city, and it eventually fell into decline. In the mid-nineteenth century, ruins of ancient Taxila were rediscovered by British archaeologist Alexander Cunningham. In 1980, UNESCO designated Taxila as a World Heritage Site.

Taxila is a historic city and World Heritage Site located in the Punjab province of Pakistan. Situated near the Indus River valley, the area has a very long history of human settlement dating back thousands of years.
pages.caption: Eastern border of the Achaemenid Empire

evidence.fileTitle: File:Eastern border of the Achaemenid Empire.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Eastern border of the Achaemenid Empire

pages.text: Throughout ancient times, Taxila served as a capital for several different civilisations and kingdoms. The Persian Achaemenid Empire, Greeks led by Alexander, and the Mauryan Empire all held control of the region at different points in history.
pages.caption: A map of Alexander's campaign in ancient India.

imageProvenance.credit: No machine-readable author provided. World Imaging assumed (based on copyright claims).

evidence.articleCaption: A map of Alexander's campaign in ancient India.

pages.text: Some scholars consider ancient Taxila to be one of the earliest educational centers in South Asia. Important historical figures such as the strategist Chanakya and the grammarian Panini are connected to the city's intellectual tradition.
pages.caption: A view over the ruins of Sirkap.

evidence.articleCaption: A view over the ruins of Sirkap.

pages.text: Following periods under Indo-Greek, Indo-Scythian, and Kushan rule, the city experienced decline after invasions by the Hunas in the fifth century. It eventually faded into obscurity until British archaeologists rediscovered the ruins in the nineteenth century.
pages.caption: The Dharmarajika Stupa

evidence.articleCaption: The Dharmarajika Stupa

pages.text: Today, Taxila is a popular tourist destination featuring multiple ancient settlement sites that reveal the pattern of urban evolution. UNESCO designated the area a World Heritage Site in 1980, and the local museum preserves artifacts found during excavations.

C1-C2.headline: Urban Evolution and Legacy of Taxila

pages.text: Taxila, historically recognized as Takshaśilā, is situated on the eastern bank of the Indus River in northern Punjab, Pakistan. Archaeological investigations indicate that the region sustained settlement activity from the Neolithic and Early Harappan periods before establishing major urban centers.
pages.caption: Eastern border of the Achaemenid Empire

evidence.fileTitle: File:Eastern border of the Achaemenid Empire.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Eastern border of the Achaemenid Empire

pages.text: As a pivotal junction between South Asia and Central Asia, the city functioned successively as a provincial capital or imperial seat under the Achaemenid Empire, the Mauryans, Indo-Greeks, Indo-Scythians, Indo-Parthians, and Kushans.
pages.caption: A map of Alexander's campaign in ancient India.

imageProvenance.credit: No machine-readable author provided. World Imaging assumed (based on copyright claims).

evidence.articleCaption: A map of Alexander's campaign in ancient India.

pages.text: While certain researchers interpret the traditional educational framework of Taxila as one of the earliest tertiary centers in the region, others note structural differences compared to later institutional universities like Nalanda. Nevertheless, the settlement exerted profound influence on Sanskrit linguistics and classical literature.
pages.caption: A view over the ruins of Sirkap.

evidence.articleCaption: A view over the ruins of Sirkap.

pages.text: The geopolitical stability of the city deteriorated following fifth-century invasions by the Kidarites and Hephthalite-associated forces, compounded by regional trade disruptions and shifting imperial conflicts. Subsequent centuries saw the site fall into progressive decline and obscurity.
pages.caption: The Dharmarajika Stupa

evidence.articleCaption: The Dharmarajika Stupa

pages.text: Nineteenth-century rediscovery and subsequent excavations by archaeologists uncovered four distinct urban settlement sites spanning multiple epochs. In recognition of its stratigraphic contribution to South Asian urban evolution, UNESCO designated Taxila a World Heritage Site in 1980.

A1-A2.headline: Canoe Routes and the Fur Trade in Canada

pages.text: Long ago, people used rivers and lakes to explore the Canadian land. Water travel was very important because the country has many rivers and short paths between them. The main business driving this exploration was the fur trade. Traders wanted beaver fur to sell in Europe.
pages.caption: A large Montreal canoe running rapids. The Avant stands in front with a steering paddle and the Gouvernail steers from the rear. The milieux provide power under the instructions of the Avant

evidence.articleCaption: A large Montreal canoe running rapids. The Avant stands in front with a steering paddle and the Gouvernail steers from the rear. The milieux provide power under the instructions of the Avant

pages.text: The St. Lawrence River was a great way to enter the continent. French fishermen started trading for furs in the sixteenth century. When Quebec was founded, traders went through many rivers and lakes to meet native people. Montreal became the main base for storing furs.
pages.caption: Major drainage basins and divides in North America

evidence.articleCaption: Major drainage basins and divides in North America

pages.text: Instead of staying on the main river, travelers used a special route west from Montreal. They went up the Ottawa River and crossed over short land paths to reach Georgian Bay. This path was called the first trans Canada highway.
pages.caption: The Saskatchewan enters Lake Winnipeg through Cedar Lake.

evidence.articleCaption: The Saskatchewan enters Lake Winnipeg through Cedar Lake.

pages.text: Voyageurs also traveled near the United States border. They used long land paths like the Grand Portage to avoid waterfalls and rivers. Their boats went through many lakes and rivers to reach Lake Winnipeg and areas further west.
pages.caption: The Saskatchewan River drains the prairies east into Lake Winnipeg.The Nelson River drains Lake Winnipeg northeast into Hudson Bay.The Red River comes in from the south.

evidence.articleCaption: The Saskatchewan River drains the prairies east into Lake Winnipeg.The Nelson River drains Lake Winnipeg northeast into Hudson Bay.The Red River comes in from the south.

pages.text: Later, explorers reached the far north and the Pacific coast. They crossed difficult land paths to find rivers flowing into the Arctic Ocean. British and Canadian traders also built routes to the west coast, where they competed with American fur companies.

B1-B2.headline: Early Canadian Canoe Routes and the Fur Trade

pages.text: European exploration of the Canadian interior relied primarily on river travel. Because the land features numerous navigable rivers connected by short portages, water-borne travel faced no serious barriers east of the Rocky Mountains. The fur trade, driven mainly by the demand for beaver pelts, financed and motivated both early exploration and initial settlement as European traders exchanged merchandise with native populations.
pages.caption: A large Montreal canoe running rapids. The Avant stands in front with a steering paddle and the Gouvernail steers from the rear. The milieux provide power under the instructions of the Avant

evidence.articleCaption: A large Montreal canoe running rapids. The Avant stands in front with a steering paddle and the Gouvernail steers from the rear. The milieux provide power under the instructions of the Avant

pages.text: While several entry points existed, the St. Lawrence River served as the primary gateway to the continent. During the French Era, cod fishermen traded for furs at Tadoussac, and the foundation of Quebec allowed coureurs des bois to spread through inland waterways. Montreal developed into the central base where furs were stored before shipment to Europe, while tribes acted as middlemen bringing pelts from further inland.
pages.caption: Major drainage basins and divides in North America

evidence.articleCaption: Major drainage basins and divides in North America

pages.text: Travelers bypassed the upper St. Lawrence rapids by taking a western route from Montreal that utilized the Ottawa and Mattawa rivers, crossed the La Vase portage, and descended the French River to Georgian Bay. Known as the first Trans-Canada Highway, this path was first used by Étienne Brûlé and Samuel de Champlain, with alternative routes available when Iroquois hostility made the Ottawa River dangerous.
pages.caption: The Saskatchewan enters Lake Winnipeg through Cedar Lake.

evidence.articleCaption: The Saskatchewan enters Lake Winnipeg through Cedar Lake.

pages.text: Further west near Lake Superior, voyageurs navigated a complex network of rivers and lakes. They utilized the nine-mile Grand Portage to bypass the Pigeon River's canyon and waterfalls, eventually reaching Lake Winnipeg via the Winnipeg River. Meanwhile, the British maintained posts on Hudson Bay, initially waiting for indigenous hunters to bring furs directly to the coast before eventually moving inland.
pages.caption: The Saskatchewan River drains the prairies east into Lake Winnipeg.The Nelson River drains Lake Winnipeg northeast into Hudson Bay.The Red River comes in from the south.

evidence.articleCaption: The Saskatchewan River drains the prairies east into Lake Winnipeg.The Nelson River drains Lake Winnipeg northeast into Hudson Bay.The Red River comes in from the south.

pages.text: Explorers eventually pushed toward the Arctic and Pacific watersheds. The route from Cumberland House led through the Churchill River basin and across the challenging Methye Portage to the Clearwater River. By the early nineteenth century, explorers like David Thompson reached the mouth of the Columbia River, linking inland canoe routes to a growing maritime fur trade on the Pacific coast.

C1-C2.headline: Waterways of Empire: Canadian Canoe Routes

pages.text: The penetration of the Canadian interior by Europeans was fundamentally contingent upon fluvial networks. Devoid of major geographic impediments east of the Rockies, the landscape offered interconnected river systems bridged by brief portages. This geographic continuity facilitated a commercial imperative: the European demand for beaver pelts catalyzed both the initial exploration and subsequent settlement.
pages.caption: A large Montreal canoe running rapids. The Avant stands in front with a steering paddle and the Gouvernail steers from the rear. The milieux provide power under the instructions of the Avant

evidence.articleCaption: A large Montreal canoe running rapids. The Avant stands in front with a steering paddle and the Gouvernail steers from the rear. The milieux provide power under the instructions of the Avant

pages.text: Geographic constraints eliminated several potential entry points, rendering the St. Lawrence River the premier access route to the continent. Following sixteenth-century cod fisheries and the establishment of Quebec, coureurs des bois utilized extensive riverine networks to trade with indigenous groups. Montreal functioned as the indispensable entrepôt for accumulating pelts prior to transatlantic shipment, while localized tribes operated as intermediaries drawing pelts from increasingly remote interior zones.
pages.caption: Major drainage basins and divides in North America

evidence.articleCaption: Major drainage basins and divides in North America

pages.text: Navigational hazards on the upper St. Lawrence necessitated an alternative westward trajectory originating near Montreal. This passage ascended the Ottawa and Mattawa rivers, traversed the La Vase portage to Lake Nipissing, and descended via the French River into Georgian Bay. Frequently designated the initial Trans-Canada Highway, this route was pioneered by Étienne Brûlé and Samuel de Champlain, with alternate diversions established to circumvent hostile indigenous territories.
pages.caption: The Saskatchewan enters Lake Winnipeg through Cedar Lake.

evidence.articleCaption: The Saskatchewan enters Lake Winnipeg through Cedar Lake.

pages.text: Operations expanded westward into the Nelson River basin, where voyageurs traversed the protracted Grand Portage to circumvent the Pigeon River canyon. Navigating a succession of boundary lakes and the Winnipeg River, expeditions unlocked access to Lake Winnipeg and the broader interior. Concurrently, British trading ventures initially adhered to coastal posts on Hudson Bay before aggressive French inland expansion compelled them to establish interior supply lines.
pages.caption: The Saskatchewan River drains the prairies east into Lake Winnipeg.The Nelson River drains Lake Winnipeg northeast into Hudson Bay.The Red River comes in from the south.

evidence.articleCaption: The Saskatchewan River drains the prairies east into Lake Winnipeg.The Nelson River drains Lake Winnipeg northeast into Hudson Bay.The Red River comes in from the south.

pages.text: Continental exploration ultimately breached northern and western boundaries. The axis extending from Cumberland House utilized the Sturgeon-Weir and Churchill river systems, culminating in the arduous transit of the Methye Portage to reach Arctic-drainage waters. Concurrently, southern and western expansions linked interior canoe pathways to the Pacific littoral, highlighted by David Thompson reaching the Columbia River and establishing a competitive presence in the Pacific fur trade.

title: The Wars and Foreign Policy of Justinian
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Emperor Justinian ruled the Roman Empire. His reign was marked by numerous wars to recover lost western territories and continue conflicts in the east. Historians know about these military campaigns thanks to the works of Procopius and other Byzantine writers who recorded the history of that era.
pages.caption: Mounted and foot Byzantine warriors on a 6th-century pyxis from the Sens Museum [fr]

evidence.articleCaption: Mounted and foot Byzantine warriors on a 6th-century pyxis from the Sens Museum [fr]

pages.text: In the west, Justinian fought barbarian kingdoms. He conquered the Vandal Kingdom in North Africa between 533 and 534. He also brought Italy under Byzantine control after a long war with the Ostrogoths from 535 to 554.
pages.caption: A 6th-century Byzantine horseman on a plate from the Isola Rizza treasure.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Piatto d'argento con scena di combattimento, dal tesoro di isola rizza, 510 dc ca. 01.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A 6th-century Byzantine horseman on a plate from the Isola Rizza treasure.

pages.text: In the east, Justinian continued a war with Persia. This conflict lasted with short breaks until 562. Byzantium also fought less successful wars in Spain against the Visigothic Kingdom. These campaigns used many resources.
pages.caption: Map of the Vandalic War campaigns

evidence.articleCaption: Map of the Vandalic War campaigns

pages.text: The Byzantine army resembled the earlier Roman army, with its field army and frontier troops. The military numbered around 150,000 men. Barbarians played a significant role in the armed forces, although modern researchers still debate the exact details and nature of their involvement.
pages.caption: Medallion commemorating the recovery of Africa

evidence.articleCaption: Medallion commemorating the recovery of Africa

pages.text: After Justinian died, the empire struggled. New peoples like the Slavs, Avars, and Lombards attacked. The army lost discipline, and epidemics caused demographic losses. Justinian's big campaigns contributed to the later decline of Byzantium.

B1-B2.headline: The Wars and Foreign Policy of Justinian

pages.text: The reign of Emperor Justinian I from 527 to 565 was defined by extensive military campaigns aimed at recovering western Mediterranean territories lost by Rome in the fifth century. Believing it was his Christian duty to restore former borders, Justinian engaged in prolonged conflicts across both the western and eastern frontiers.
pages.caption: Mounted and foot Byzantine warriors on a 6th-century pyxis from the Sens Museum [fr]

evidence.articleCaption: Mounted and foot Byzantine warriors on a 6th-century pyxis from the Sens Museum [fr]

pages.text: In the west, his armies conquered the Vandal Kingdom in North Africa from 533 to 534 and brought Italy under Byzantine control following a destructive war with the Ostrogoths between 535 and 554. His forces also expanded Byzantine possessions in Spain through less successful wars against the Visigothic Kingdom.
pages.caption: A 6th-century Byzantine horseman on a plate from the Isola Rizza treasure.

pages.text: Meanwhile, in the east, Justinian maintained hostilities with the Sasanian Empire of Persia. This intermittent conflict continued until 562. Much of our knowledge of these events comes from Procopius and other contemporary Byzantine historians who carefully documented the emperor's campaigns.

pages.text: The Byzantine military resembled earlier Roman structures, featuring field armies and frontier troops totaling roughly 150,000 men. Barbarians constituted a substantial component of these forces, though their exact role and recruitment remain a subject of scholarly debate among researchers.
pages.caption: Medallion commemorating the recovery of Africa

evidence.articleCaption: Medallion commemorating the recovery of Africa

pages.text: Despite destroying kingdoms like the Vandals and Ostrogoths, Justinian's conquests drained imperial resources. By ignoring sixth-century realities, his campaigns left the empire vulnerable to new groups like the Slavs, Avars, and Lombards, ultimately contributing to the long-term decline of Byzantium.

Characterized by ambitious reconquests, the reign of Justinian I between 527 and 565 sought to reinstate the fifth-century territorial boundaries of the Roman Empire. Viewing state restoration as an imperial Christian obligation, Justinian prosecuted concurrent conflicts along both western and eastern geopolitical horizons, documented extensively by Procopius and other historians.
pages.caption: Mounted and foot Byzantine warriors on a 6th-century pyxis from the Sens Museum [fr]

evidence.articleCaption: Mounted and foot Byzantine warriors on a 6th-century pyxis from the Sens Museum [fr]

pages.text: Western interventions achieved notable victories, including the subjugation of the Vandal Kingdom in North Africa from 533 to 534 and the incorporation of Italy following protracted hostilities with the Ostrogoths between 535 and 554. Concurrently, marginally successful campaigns against the Visigothic Kingdom expanded Byzantine footholds in Spain.
pages.caption: A 6th-century Byzantine horseman on a plate from the Isola Rizza treasure.

pages.text: Along the eastern frontier, Justinian sustained protracted hostilities against the Sasanian Empire, persisting with intermittent truces until 562. These campaigns operated alongside complex diplomatic interactions, including a rejected Persian proposal during the mid-520s regarding imperial succession and the integration of the shah's son.

pages.text: The contemporary Byzantine military apparatus comprised approximately 150,000 personnel distributed between mobile field forces and frontier units. Barbarian mercenaries and federated troops constituted a prominent yet debated demographic within these armed forces, which relied on administrative structures reminiscent of earlier Roman military organization.

evidence.articleCaption: Medallion commemorating the recovery of Africa

pages.text: Although Justinian successfully dismantled several barbarian states, his aggressive foreign policy strained imperial demographics and resources. By failing to adapt to emergent threats from groups such as the Slavs and Lombards, his campaigns are widely considered to have catalyzed the subsequent administrative and military decline of Byzantium.
